text: Earth is getting warmer mainly because people are burning coal, oil and natural gas. Burning them releases [[@carbon-cycle|carbon dioxide]], a gas that traps heat in the air, like a blanket around the planet. [[@forests-india|Cutting down forests]] adds more.

Since the late 1800s, Earth's average temperature has risen by about 1.3 °C, according to a 2024 estimate by the World Meteorological Organization. That sounds small, but it is an average across the whole planet, all year round. It is already melting glaciers, raising the sea and making [[@heatwaves|heatwaves]] more common.

myth: Global warming is caused by the hole in the ozone layer.

They are two different problems. The ozone hole lets in more harmful ultraviolet light. Global warming is caused mainly by carbon dioxide and other gases that trap heat. The two are only loosely linked.

sec.t:
Sunlight passes through the air and warms the ground and the sea. The warm Earth then gives off heat as invisible infrared light. Some gases in the air, especially carbon dioxide, water vapour and methane, absorb that heat and send part of it back down. These are called [[greenhouse-gas|greenhouse gases]].

This is natural, and it is a good thing. Without any greenhouse gases, Earth would be about 33 °C colder, and mostly frozen. The problem is that people have added much more of them, so the blanket has grown thicker.

In 1856, the American scientist Eunice Foote filled glass jars with different gases and set them in the sun. The jar with carbon dioxide got the hottest. She wrote that more of this gas in the air would make Earth warmer. A few years later, the Irish scientist John Tyndall measured how gases absorb heat in more detail.

In 1958, Charles David Keeling began measuring carbon dioxide on Mauna Loa in [[@hawaii-islands|Hawaii]], far from cities and factories. His measurements, continued to this day, form a famous rising zigzag called the Keeling Curve. Before factories, the air held about 280 parts per million of carbon dioxide. Now it holds more than 420.

Most [[@glaciers|glaciers]] are shrinking, from Alaska to the Himalaya. Arctic sea ice at the end of summer covers far less area than it did when [[@satellites-help|satellites]] began watching it in the late 1970s. As ice on land melts and warm water expands, the sea has risen by about 20 cm since 1900, and it is [[@sea-level-rise|rising faster now]].

Heatwaves are hotter and more frequent in many places, including India and the United States. [[@ocean-and-climate|Warm oceans]] can make [[@coral-reefs|coral reefs]] turn white and die. The ten warmest years on record have all happened since 2015.

In 2015, almost every country agreed in Paris to try to keep warming well below 2 °C. Countries are building [[@renewable-energy|solar farms]], [[@wind-turbines|wind turbines]] and electric buses, and finding [[@green-tech|new technology]] to use less energy. India has set up some of the world's largest solar parks, such as Bhadla in Rajasthan.

People disagree about how fast to change and who should pay, and countries are at very different stages. Those are questions of fairness and politics. The science of why Earth is warming is much more settled.

One cold winter doesn't mean warming has stopped, and one hot summer doesn't prove it. Weather is what happens day to day. Climate is the pattern over 30 years or more. Scientists look at the long trend across the whole planet, and that trend points clearly upward.

text: Under Yellowstone National Park in the USA there is hot [[magma|magma]]. Rain and snowmelt soak into the ground and are heated by it. In a geyser, the water collects in a narrow underground pipe.

Deep down, the weight of the water above squeezes the hot water, so it can't boil even above 100°C. When a little water near the top turns to steam and escapes, the squeeze drops, and all the super-hot water flashes into steam at once. Whoosh.

st.reveal: Pressure raises the boiling point. Deep down, the water is squeezed by everything above it, so it can get super-hot without boiling, until it suddenly flashes into steam.

myth: Old Faithful erupts exactly once an hour, like clockwork.

The gap between eruptions varies, usually from about an hour to nearly two. Park rangers predict the next one from how long the last eruption lasted. A long eruption empties the pipe more, so the wait afterwards is longer.

sec.h: A pressure cooker in the ground
sec.t:
It works a bit like a pressure cooker. In a sealed cooker, extra pressure lets water get hotter than 100 °C without [[@boiling-water|boiling]]. Inside a geyser, the pressure comes from the column of water above. Even a few metres of water adds enough squeeze to raise the boiling point.

As heat keeps flowing up from below, the deep water gets hotter and hotter. Eventually some of it boils anyway. Bubbles push water out of the top, the weight above drops, and the super-hot water below suddenly boils in a rush. The eruption keeps going until the pipe is nearly empty. Then it slowly refills, and the cycle starts again.

Old Faithful got its name because it erupts so regularly: about every 60 to 110 minutes. Each blast lasts a few minutes and reaches up to about 55 metres, taller than a 15-storey building. A single eruption throws out roughly 14,000 to 32,000 litres of water, enough to fill a small tanker truck.

It was named in 1870 by members of an expedition exploring the area, who were struck by how reliably it went off. Today park rangers predict each eruption, and crowds gather on wooden boardwalks to watch.

A geyser needs three things at once: plenty of underground heat, a steady supply of water, and a narrow, sealed pipe of rock. The pipe is often lined with a hard mineral called silica, left behind by the hot water itself. Without all three, you get a gentle hot spring or a [[@earth-mud-volcanoes|bubbling mud pot]] instead.

That's why fewer than a thousand geysers exist on Earth, and about half are in Yellowstone. The word "geyser" comes from Geysir, a famous spouting spring in [[@iceland|Iceland]]. India has many [[@geysers-hot-springs|hot springs]], such as Manikaran in [[@himachal|Himachal Pradesh]], but no geysers like Old Faithful.

Some of Yellowstone's hot springs are ringed with bright bands of orange, yellow and green. These colours come from microbes, tiny living things that thrive in water hot enough to scald you.

In the 1960s, a scientist named Thomas Brock found one of them, a bacterium called *Thermus aquaticus*, in a Yellowstone hot spring. Years later, a substance from it became the key ingredient in a test that copies DNA, used in labs everywhere, including for COVID-19 tests. Even the [[@microbes-friendly|smallest living things]] can turn out to be helpful.

text: Yes, but only by a tiny amount. Time doesn't tick at the same rate everywhere. It runs slightly slower for things that move very fast, and slightly faster where gravity is weaker. Both ideas come from [[@einstein|Albert Einstein]].

On the [[@space-station|International Space Station]], the speed effect wins. The station races around Earth at about 28,000 km/h, so its clocks run a little slow compared with clocks on the ground. An astronaut who spends a year up there ages less than a hundredth of a second less than someone at home. It is far too small to feel, but extremely precise clocks can measure it.

st.reveal: The station moves so fast that its clocks tick very slightly slower than clocks on the ground. Over a year, that adds up to less than a hundredth of a second. Real, measurable, and far too small to notice.

To them, the ball traces a row of arches, a longer path. Einstein used a similar idea, with light instead of a ball, to show why moving clocks run slow.
myth: Astronauts come back from long missions years younger than their friends.

The difference is real but tiny, a few hundredths of a second at most, even for people who have spent more than three years in orbit. Big time differences only happen at speeds close to the speed of light or near something like a black hole.

sec.t:
In 1905, Einstein worked out something very strange. The speed of light is the same for everyone, however fast they are moving. For that to be true, time itself has to stretch for moving objects. The faster something moves, the slower its clocks tick, compared with someone standing still.

At everyday speeds, the effect is almost zero. Even on a jet plane it amounts to billionths of a second. But for particles racing near the speed of light, time stretches hugely. Scientists see this every day in particle accelerators, where fast-moving particles survive far longer than slow ones before breaking down.

In 1971, two American scientists, Joseph Hafele and Richard Keating, carried four atomic clocks around the world on ordinary passenger flights, first heading east and then west. Then they compared them with clocks left behind at the US Naval Observatory in Washington. The travelling clocks had gained or lost tiny amounts of time, from tens to hundreds of billionths of a second, roughly as Einstein's theories predicted.

That might sound like a strange use of airline seats, but it was one of the first direct tests of these ideas using real [[@clocks|clocks]].

[[@gps-how|GPS]] [[@satellites-help|satellites]] orbit about 20,200 km up. They move fast, which slows their clocks. But they are also far from Earth, where gravity is weaker, which speeds them up more. Overall, their clocks gain about 38 millionths of a second every day.

If engineers did not correct for this, GPS positions would drift by about 10 km a day, and your map app would soon be useless. So every time you see your blue dot in the right place, Einstein's ideas are being put to work.

From 2015 to 2016, NASA astronaut Scott Kelly spent almost a year on the space station while his identical [[@twins|twin]], Mark, a retired astronaut, stayed on Earth. Doctors studied both brothers to see how space changes the body.

The time difference was only a few thousandths of a second. The study found more interesting changes in Scott's body, such as in his eyes and immune system, most of which went back to normal after he came home.

The Russian cosmonaut Oleg Kononenko has spent more than 1,000 days in orbit, more than anyone else. Even so, by this calculation he is only a few hundredths of a second younger than he would otherwise be.

sec.h: Could you travel into the future?
sec.t: In a way, yes. A spaceship travelling at nearly the speed of light could return after what felt like a few years to its crew, while decades had passed on Earth. Nobody can build such a ship. But the physics says it would work, and every second on the space station proves the idea in a small way.

text: Hundreds of people have now been to space, and women have been part of the story almost from the beginning. Valentina Tereshkova of the Soviet Union went first, in 1963. The USA's first woman, Sally Ride, flew in 1983.

Since then, women have commanded the [[@space-station|International Space Station]], repaired telescopes, done spacewalks and, in 2026, flown around the Moon. India's story includes [[@kalpana-chawla|Kalpana Chawla]], who flew twice on the Space Shuttle, and Sunita Williams, an American astronaut with family roots in Gujarat.
Each of them had to be a scientist, engineer or pilot first. Getting picked is hard for anyone. For women in the early decades, it was harder still.

sec.t:
Tereshkova worked in a textile factory and spent her spare time jumping out of planes with a local club. The Soviet space programme wanted parachutists, because its capsules didn't land gently. Cosmonauts had to eject and float down on their own.

On 16 June 1963 she launched on Vostok 6. She circled Earth 48 times in almost three days, more time in orbit than all of America's astronauts had managed together until then. Her call sign was *Chaika*, which means seagull.

Another woman didn't fly for nineteen years, until Svetlana Savitskaya in 1982. In 1984, Savitskaya became the first woman to walk in space.

When NASA picked its first astronauts in 1959, it chose only military test pilots, and the armed forces didn't let women fly jets. Women weren't selected until 1978. Sally Ride, a physicist from California, was one of six women in that group.

She flew on the Space Shuttle Challenger in June 1983. Reporters asked whether she would cry if things went wrong. She answered calmly and got on with the job. In 1992, Mae Jemison, a doctor and engineer, became the first African American woman in space.

Behind them were women who never flew but made flight possible, such as the [[@maths-history-women|mathematicians who calculated orbits]] by hand.

{{story:moon-race-women}}

Kalpana Chawla grew up in Karnal, Haryana, and loved aeroplanes. She studied aeronautical engineering in Chandigarh, then moved to the USA. In 1997 she flew on the Space Shuttle Columbia, becoming the first woman born in India to go to space. She died with her six crewmates when Columbia broke apart on its return in 2003. Schools, scholarships and a satellite have been named after her.

Sunita Williams has done nine spacewalks. In 2024 she flew to the space station on a test flight of Boeing's Starliner capsule. Problems with the capsule meant she stayed about nine months instead of about a week, returning in March 2025.

Christina Koch spent 328 days in space in 2019 and 2020, the longest single trip by a woman. During that stay, she and Jessica Meir made the first spacewalk with only women outside.

Peggy Whitson, a biochemist from Iowa, has spent about 695 days in space over her career, more than any other American or any woman. She was the first woman to command the space station.

In April 2026, Koch flew on Artemis II with three male crewmates. Their Orion capsule looped around the far side of the Moon, and the crew travelled farther from Earth than any humans before them. She became the first woman to leave low Earth orbit and see the Moon up close.

India is preparing its own crewed flights under [[@gaganyaan|Gaganyaan]]. Its first uncrewed test flight, still waiting to launch in late 2026, is due to carry a humanoid robot with a woman's face called Vyommitra, which means "space friend".

text: A fishing kingfisher sits very still on a branch or wire above the water, watching. When it spots a small fish near the surface, it dives head first, wings folded back, and seizes the fish in its dagger-shaped beak. The whole dive takes about a second. It flies back to its perch, beats the fish against the branch to stun it, and swallows it head first so the fins and scales slide down easily.
To pull this off, a kingfisher must see through the glare on the water, aim for a fish that isn't quite where it looks, and hit the water without hurting itself. Its body is built for all three.

sec.t:
When light passes from water into air, it bends. This is called [[refraction|refraction]], and it makes underwater things look shallower and in a different place than they really are. A kingfisher must allow for this, aiming below where the fish appears.

Young kingfishers miss often and get better with practice. They also tend to dive steeply from right above, where the bending is smallest. A see-through third eyelid, called a nictitating membrane, slides across each eye as it hits the water, like a pair of swimming goggles.

A kingfisher's long, sharp beak cuts into the water with hardly a splash. Its head and beak are shaped so that it slips from air into water, which is much thicker, without a big jolt. Its feathers are thick and waterproof, and after each dive it shakes off the water and preens.

The pied kingfisher, a black-and-white bird common over Indian rivers and lakes, can hunt without a perch. It hovers in one spot over open water, beating its wings fast, then plunges straight down. This lets it fish in the middle of wide lakes far from any branch.

sec.t:
India has about 12 kinds of kingfisher. The common kingfisher, only about 16 cm long, flashes electric blue and orange along streams and ponds. The white-throated kingfisher, with its chocolate-brown head and loud rattling call, is often seen on wires in towns and fields, far from water. The big stork-billed kingfisher hunts in [[@mangroves|mangroves]] and forest rivers.

That flashing blue isn't paint. Kingfisher feathers have no blue pigment at all. Inside each feather are tiny structures, much smaller than a hair is wide, that scatter blue light back towards your eye, a bit like the way the sky looks blue. If you crush a blue feather, the structure breaks and the colour turns dull grey-brown. The orange on the bird's chest, by contrast, does come from pigment.

Kingfishers usually nest in tunnels they dig into earth banks along rivers, pecking and kicking out the soil. The tunnel is often more than half a metre long. The eggs are laid in a chamber at the end. In the USA, the belted kingfisher is the one most people see, rattling along rivers and lakes. To spot any of them, walk slowly near clean water in [[@wetlands|wetlands]] and watch the branches and wires just above the surface.

text: An octopus's skin is packed with tiny colour cells called chromatophores. Each is a small, stretchy sac full of pigment, yellow, orange, red, brown or black, with little muscles all around it. When the brain sends a signal along a nerve, the muscles pull, the sac stretches into a coloured disc, and that patch of skin changes colour. When the muscles relax, the sac shrinks back to a dot.

Because these cells are controlled directly by nerves, they work very fast, often in less than a second. Below them sit other layers of cells that reflect and scatter light, adding shimmering blues, greens and bright whites.

st.reveal: Each colour cell, or chromatophore, is a stretchy sac of pigment ringed by tiny muscles. Nerves from the brain tell the muscles to pull, stretching the sac into a wide coloured disc. When they relax, it shrinks to a tiny dot.

d.try: Draw lots of small dots with a felt pen on a deflated balloon. Then blow it up slowly and watch the dots spread into big patches of colour. Let the air out and they shrink. An octopus's colour cells work in a similar way, except muscles do the stretching.
myth: Octopuses change colour only to hide.

Camouflage is a big reason, but not the only one. Octopuses also flash colours to warn predators, to scare prey, to signal to other octopuses, and their colours shift with their mood. Some even change colour while asleep.

sec.t:
The top layer is the chromatophores, which add warm colours. Under them are iridophores, which reflect light like the inside of a shell or a soap bubble, giving blues and greens. At the bottom are leucophores, white cells that scatter whatever light falls on them, so they look the colour of the surroundings.

By opening some chromatophores and closing others, an octopus can make stripes, spots, blotches or a smooth wash of colour. It can even make dark bands ripple across its body, like clouds passing over a field.

Colour is only half the trick. An octopus can also change the texture of its skin. Small bumps called papillae rise up into spikes or ridges, so it can look like rough rock, seaweed or coral. Because it has no bones, it can flatten itself against a reef or squeeze into a crack the width of its beak.

Put together, colour, pattern and shape make it one of the best disguise artists in the sea. Divers have swum right past octopuses sitting in the open.

In 2023, scientists in Japan filmed octopuses sleeping in tanks. Most of the time they were pale and still. But roughly every hour, they went into a short "active" sleep, with their skin flickering through the patterns they use when awake. The researchers suggested the brain might be replaying the day, a little like dreaming, though nobody can ask an octopus.

{{story:camouflage}}

Here is the strange part. Most octopuses have only one type of light-sensing cell in their eyes. Animals like that usually can't tell colours apart. Yet octopuses match their background beautifully.

Scientists are testing a few ideas. In 2015, researchers in California found that octopus skin itself contains light-sensitive proteins called opsins, the same kind used in eyes. A patch of skin cut off from the brain still reacted to light. So the skin may "see" brightness in its own simple way. Another idea is that the octopus's oddly shaped pupils might help it pick up colour clues by focusing different colours slightly differently. Neither idea is fully proven.

Octopuses also use colour to talk and to bluff. An angry or frightened octopus may suddenly turn dark or flash pale. The small blue-ringed octopus of the Pacific and Indian Oceans shows bright blue rings as a warning that it is extremely venomous.

The mimic octopus, discovered in 1998 off the coast of Sulawesi in Indonesia, goes further. It can change its colour and posture to imitate a striped lionfish, a sea snake or a flatfish, all animals that predators tend to avoid. And an octopus's brain doesn't do all the work. It has about 500 million nerve cells, but most of them are in its eight [[@octopus-smart|arms]], which help control the skin nearby.

Other animals change colour too, but usually more slowly. [[@lizards|Chameleons]] mostly do it by changing the spacing of tiny crystals in their skin, which can take seconds or minutes. Octopuses, squid and cuttlefish are among the fastest colour-changers known. And when a disguise fails, an octopus has a backup plan: a dark cloud of [[@octopus-ink|ink]] to cover its escape.

text: Four kinds of bear live in India: the sloth bear, the Asiatic black bear, the Himalayan brown bear and the sun bear. Each lives in a different part of the country, from hot central forests to snowy mountain meadows.

The sloth bear is the one most Indians are likely to come across in a forest, and it is found across much of the country. The black bear and brown bear live in the Himalaya, and the small sun bear lives only in the forests of the Northeast. India has no polar bears, and no giant pandas.

sec.t:
Sloth bears have long, scruffy black coats, pale snouts and a cream-coloured V or U on the chest. Their curved claws, up to about 8 centimetres long, are made for digging into hard [[@termite-mounds|termite mounds]]. Early European naturalists saw them hanging from branches and thought they were related to sloths, which is how they got the name.

Their trick is suction. A sloth bear is missing its two middle upper front teeth, so its lips and mouth work like a vacuum tube. The slurping can be heard from far away. They also love fruit and [[@honey|honey]], and they climb trees to raid beehives.

Sloth bear mothers do something few other bears do: they carry their cubs on their backs, sometimes for months. The cubs cling to the fur as the mother walks.

{{story:honey}}

The Asiatic black bear has a big white V on its chest, which gives it the name "moon bear". It lives in forests from [[@kashmir|Kashmir]] across the Himalaya to the Northeast. It eats acorns, fruit, insects and sometimes crops, which can lead to conflict with farmers.

The Himalayan brown bear is larger and lives higher up, in meadows and rocky slopes of [[@ladakh|Ladakh]], Kashmir and Himachal Pradesh. In winter, food runs out. So brown bears and some black bears sleep through the coldest months in dens, a long rest called [[hibernation|hibernation]]. Sloth bears and sun bears, which live in warmer places, don't need to.

The sun bear is the smallest bear in the world, roughly the size of a large dog. In India it is found only in a few northeastern states, such as Mizoram and Arunachal Pradesh, and it is rarely seen. It has a golden patch on its chest that looks like a rising sun.

Sun bears have very long tongues, which they poke into holes in trees to lick out insects and honey. They spend lots of time climbing and even build nests of branches high in trees.

Bears and people often share the same forests, and that can be risky for both. Sloth bears are not usually hunters of people, but when startled at close range they may attack to defend themselves or their cubs. In parts of central India, many villagers have been injured this way while collecting firewood or flowers in the forest.

Forest departments teach villagers to walk in groups, carry a torch at night and make noise along forest paths. Black bears in the Himalaya sometimes raid maize fields and apple orchards, and some states pay farmers for damaged crops. Protecting bears means keeping forests healthy, with enough fruit, insects and honey that the bears have no reason to wander into villages.

For centuries, some travelling performers in India caught sloth bear cubs, pierced their snouts and trained them to "dance" on ropes in the street. It was cruel, and it was banned under India's wildlife laws. Groups such as Wildlife SOS worked with the government and the performers' families to rescue the bears and help the families find other jobs. India's last known dancing bear was rescued in 2009.

Many rescued bears live at sanctuaries near Agra and Bengaluru. Wild sloth bears are also protected in reserves such as Daroji in [[@karnataka|Karnataka]], near Hampi, where they roam among giant boulders. Sloth bears can be grumpy when surprised, so forest villagers often talk or sing loudly while walking to warn them.

text: Pet cats come from the African wildcat, a small, striped wild cat that still lives in North Africa and the Middle East. Around 10,000 years ago, people in the Middle East began [[@farming-began|farming]] and storing grain. Grain stores attracted mice and rats, and the mice attracted wildcats.

The cats that were bold enough to hunt around villages, and calm enough to put up with people, got plenty to eat. People were happy to have pest control. Over many generations, these village cats became tamer.
So unlike dogs, cats were probably never trained or herded. They mostly chose to live with us, and they changed far less than dogs did along the way.

st.prompt: Pet cats meow a lot. Who do adult cats meow at most?

options.t: Other cats
People
Mice and birds

st.reveal: Kittens meow to their mothers, but grown-up cats mostly talk to each other with smells, body language, hisses and growls. Meowing seems to be a habit cats keep up mainly for us, perhaps because it gets results.

Most adult cats can't digest the sugar in milk well, and it can upset their stomachs. Fresh water and proper cat food are what they need.

sec.h: A cat buried with a person
sec.t:
The oldest clue comes from the island of Cyprus. At a village site called Shillourokambos, archaeologists found a cat buried close to a person, about 9,500 years ago.

Wildcats don't live naturally on Cyprus, so people must have carried cats there by boat. Taking a wild animal across the sea, and burying it near a person, suggests the cats were already special to them.

Cats also lived in villages in China about 5,300 years ago. But DNA showed those were leopard cats, a different wild species. That early partnership didn't last, and today's pet cats in China, like everywhere else, come from the African wildcat.

Ancient DNA shows that cats spread in two big waves. The first moved with early farmers from the Middle East into Europe. Later, cats from Egypt spread along sea [[@trade-routes|trade routes]], carried on ships to keep rats away from food and cargo.

Ship's cats travelled with Romans, [[@vikings|Vikings]] and European explorers. That is how cats reached the Americas, Australia and many islands. The tabby pattern with swirls and blotches, now very common, only became widespread in the Middle Ages.

A pet cat's body has barely changed from a wildcat's. It still hunts by sitting very still, then pouncing. Its eyes work best at dawn and dusk, the times when mice are most active. Many pet cats can survive on their own if they have to.

What did change was their behaviour. Pet cats are calmer around people and other cats. Grown-up cats rarely meow at each other, but they meow at people a lot, perhaps because it works.

In India, cats turn up in old stories. In the [[@panchatantra-tales|Panchatantra]], a sly cat pretends to be a holy judge so that two quarrelling animals come close enough to catch. India also has its own wild relatives, like the Asiatic wildcat of the [[@desert-life|Thar Desert]] and the jungle cat.

Cats are skilled hunters, and that can be a problem. On islands where birds and small animals never met a cat, pet and stray cats have helped wipe out some species. In the USA, studies suggest outdoor cats kill billions of birds every year.

That is why some wildlife experts ask owners to keep cats indoors, especially at night. The cat that moved in for the mice is still, at heart, a wildcat.

text: Dogs come from [[@wolves-india|grey wolves]]. Sometime before about 15,000 years ago, during the last [[@ice-ages|Ice Age]], some wolves began living near groups of human hunters. Over many generations, the wolves that were calmer around people did better. They got more food, had more pups and passed on their friendlier nature.
Slowly, those wolves changed. Their faces became shorter, their teeth smaller and their behaviour softer. They became dogs.

Nobody knows exactly where it happened. Europe, Siberia and East Asia have all been suggested, and it may have happened more than once. What is clear is that dogs were the first animal people tamed, thousands of years before cows, goats or cats, and before the first [[@farming-began|farms]].

st.prompt: In an experiment in Russia, scientists bred only the tamest foxes, generation after generation. What happened?

options.t: Nothing changed except that they were calmer
They began to wag their tails, and some had floppy ears and patchy coats
They grew much bigger than wild foxes

st.reveal: Within a few dozen generations, the tame foxes whined for attention and wagged their tails like dogs. Some had floppy ears, curly tails and patches of white fur. Picking for friendliness alone brought a whole bundle of dog-like changes.

myth: Dogs see the world only in black and white.
Dogs do see colour, just fewer colours than most people. They see blues and yellows well, but reds and greens look much alike to them, a bit like a person with red-green colour blindness.

hundreds of millions, against about 5 million in yours

sec.t:
For a long time, people imagined Stone Age hunters taking wolf pups home and raising them. That may have happened. But many scientists now think the wolves did much of the work themselves.

Hunters left bones and scraps around their camps. Wolves brave enough to come close, but not so aggressive that people drove them off, got an easy meal. Over time, these camp wolves became a separate group. In return, they may have warned people of danger and helped track animals. This is sometimes called self-domestication.

The oldest burial that is clearly a dog was found at Bonn-Oberkassel in Germany. About 14,000 years ago, a young dog was buried there with two people. It had been seriously ill as a puppy, and it seems people nursed it for weeks before it died.

{{story:stone-age}}

In 1959, a Russian scientist named Dmitry Belyaev began a famous experiment in Siberia. He bred silver foxes, keeping only the ones that were least afraid of people.

After a few dozen generations, the foxes wagged their tails, licked their keepers and whined for attention. Some had floppy ears, curly tails and white patches, just like many dogs. Choosing for friendliness alone seemed to bring along a whole set of changes. It gave scientists a clue to how wolves might have turned into dogs.

Dogs are unusually good at reading people. Even young puppies will follow a pointing finger to find hidden food. Dogs also look at our faces for clues, and they have a small muscle above each eye that lifts the inner eyebrow. That creates the sad "puppy-dog eyes" that people find so hard to resist. Most wolves don't have it.

Dogs changed in their insides too. When people started farming, dogs living with them ate more grain scraps. Over time, many dogs gained extra copies of a gene that helps digest starch, something wolves do poorly.

And they kept their superb sense of smell. [[@power-dogs-nose|A dog's nose]] has hundreds of millions of smell sensors, compared with about five million in yours, as explained in [[@nose-smell|how noses work]].

In 1925, sled dog teams raced medicine across frozen [[@alaska|Alaska]] to the town of Nome, to stop an outbreak of a deadly disease. In 1957, a Moscow street dog named Laika became the first animal to orbit Earth, aboard Sputnik 2. She did not survive the flight.

In India, the Mahabharata ends with a dog. As Yudhishthira climbs towards heaven, only a faithful dog stays with him. He refuses to enter heaven without it, and the dog turns out to be the god Dharma in disguise.

Most modern breeds are young, created in the last 200 years. India has its own old types, like the Rajapalayam and the Mudhol hound, and the hardy Indian street dog, whose roots may go back thousands of years. All of them still share most of their DNA with wolves, like the [[@yellowstone-wolves|wolves of Yellowstone]].

text: Mosquitoes find people mostly by smell. They follow the carbon dioxide you breathe out, then home in on your body heat and the scent of your skin. Your skin smell is a mix of chemicals made by your body and by the bacteria that live on it, and it's a little different for everyone.

Some people's mix is far more attractive to mosquitoes than others'. Scientists have found that people who make more of certain fatty acids on their skin get bitten more, and they stay that way for years. Other things matter too: people who breathe out more carbon dioxide, are hot from running, or are wearing dark clothes are easier for mosquitoes to find.

st.prompt: Which mosquitoes bite people?

options.t: Only the females
Only the males
Both, equally

st.reveal: Both males and females drink flower nectar for energy. Only females bite, because they need the protein in blood to make their eggs.

src: World Health Organization, World Malaria Report 2024.

d.try: Keep a family bite diary for one week. Each evening, everyone counts any new mosquito bites and notes what colour clothes they wore and whether they had been running around. At the end of the week, make a simple chart and see who the "mosquito magnet" is.
myth: Mosquitoes bite some people more because they have sweet blood.
Mosquitoes can't taste your blood before they bite. They choose you by the carbon dioxide you breathe out, your warmth and the smell of your skin, which is shaped by the bacteria living on it.
facts: carbon dioxide, body heat and skin smell

sec.t:
Male mosquitoes never bite. Both males and females drink nectar from flowers for energy. But a female needs the protein in blood to make her eggs. After a meal of blood, she can lay a batch of 100 or more eggs in still water.

There are about 3,500 kinds of mosquito, and most don't bite people at all. A few, such as Aedes and Anopheles mosquitoes, are very good at finding humans. These are the ones that spread [[@mosquito-diseases|diseases like dengue and malaria]].

In 2022, researchers at Rockefeller University in New York tested how attractive different people's smells were to mosquitoes. Volunteers wore nylon stockings on their arms for six hours to collect their skin scent. Then the stockings were placed in a box with mosquitoes.

Some people's stockings attracted many times more mosquitoes than others'. When the volunteers were tested again over months and years, the "magnets" stayed magnets. Their skin had higher levels of certain fatty acids. Nobody yet knows how to change your own natural scent.

People who breathe out more carbon dioxide, like adults compared with small children, are often bitten more. Pregnant women tend to be bitten more too, probably because they breathe out more and are slightly warmer.

Colour makes a difference. A 2022 study found that once mosquitoes smelled carbon dioxide, they flew towards red, orange, black and cyan colours, and ignored green, blue and white. Blood type is less clear. Some studies suggest mosquitoes prefer people with type O blood, but others found no difference.

In 1897, a British army doctor named Ronald Ross, working in Secunderabad, near Hyderabad, found the malaria parasite in the stomach of an Anopheles mosquito. It proved that mosquitoes spread malaria. He won the Nobel Prize in 1902 for this work.

Malaria still kills about 6 lakh people a year, mostly young children in Africa, according to the World Health Organization's 2023 figures. That is why scientists care so much about what attracts mosquitoes. A better understanding of mosquito [[@nose-smell|smell]] could lead to better repellents and traps.

Repellents work by confusing the mosquito's sense of smell. Long sleeves, mosquito nets, window screens and getting rid of standing water in pots and buckets all help. Studies have found that eating garlic doesn't keep mosquitoes away, despite what many people believe. If a bite becomes very swollen or someone gets a fever after being bitten, tell a trusted adult, who can check with a doctor.

text: When the wind blows from behind, a sail simply catches it like a parachute and the boat is pushed along. That part is easy. The clever part is going against the wind.

When a sail is set at an angle to the wind, it curves like [[@made-planes|an aeroplane wing]] standing on its edge. Air flowing around the curved sail is bent and speeds up on one side, and the sail is pushed sideways and slightly forwards. This push is called [[lift|lift]]. Underneath the boat, a fin called a keel grips the water and stops the boat sliding sideways. With sideways movement blocked, the push turns into forward motion.
No boat can sail straight into the wind. But most can sail at about 45 degrees to it, so they zigzag their way upwind.

st.prompt: A sailor wants to reach a buoy directly upwind. What do they do?

options.t: Point straight at the buoy and pull the sail in tight
Zigzag towards it at an angle to the wind
Wait for the wind to change

st.reveal: No sailboat can go straight into the wind, because the sail just flaps. But it can sail at about 45 degrees to the wind, first one way and then the other. This zigzag is called tacking, and it gets the boat upwind step by step.

d.try: Float a lid or a flat piece of foam in a tub of water, with a paper sail stuck on a straw. Blow gently from behind, then from the side. Then glue a strip of card under the boat as a keel and blow from the side again. See how the keel helps the boat go forward instead of sliding away.
myth: A sailboat can only go where the wind blows it.

A sail works like a wing, producing a sideways push that the keel turns into forward motion. Sailboats can travel across the wind and even upwind, by zigzagging. Only the zone straight into the wind is off-limits.
facts: a fin under the boat that stops it sliding sideways
a triangular sail used on Indian Ocean dhows for centuries
a sailing race first held in 1851

sec.t:
An [[@airplanes-fly|aeroplane wing]] is shaped and tilted so that air moving past it is bent downwards. Pushing the air down pushes the wing up. A sail does the same thing sideways. It bends the wind, and the wind pushes back on the sail.

On its own, that sideways push would just shove the boat across the water like a leaf. The keel stops it. Think of squeezing a slippery orange seed between your fingers: you press from the sides, and the seed shoots forward. The sail presses from one side, the keel resists from the other, and the boat squirts forward between them.

For centuries, sailors in the Arabian Sea and the Indian Ocean used a triangular sail called a lateen sail on wooden boats known as dhows. A lateen sail can be set closer to the wind than a square sail, so dhows could sail across and partly against the wind.

Traders also learned to use the [[@monsoon|monsoon]]. Winds blowing from the south-west in summer carried ships from Arabia and East Africa towards India, and north-east winds in winter took them back. These seasonal [[@trade-routes|trade routes]] carried spices, cotton, horses and ideas for well over a thousand years. Wooden dhows are still built by hand in places like Mandvi in Gujarat.

Modern racing boats push the idea to extremes. The America's Cup, a sailing race first held off England in 1851, now uses boats that rise out of the water on thin underwater wings called foils. With less water dragging on the hull, they can race at two or three times the wind's speed.

This sounds impossible, but it isn't. When a boat sails across the wind, its own speed creates extra wind over the sail, the way you feel a breeze on a bicycle even on a still day. Ice yachts and land yachts, which roll or skate with little friction, can go even faster compared with the wind. A [[@kite-flying|kite]] climbs into a breeze using a similar mix of lift and a tight string.

text: A candle is a small fuel factory. The heat of the flame melts a pool of wax at the top of the candle. The wick soaks up that liquid wax and carries it upwards, the way a strip of cloth soaks up spilt water.

Near the flame, the liquid wax gets so hot that it turns into a gas. That gas mixes with oxygen from the air and burns. The burning makes more heat, which melts more wax, and the cycle keeps going until the wax runs out.
So the solid candle you hold is a store of fuel. Only the thin, invisible layer of wax gas around the wick is ever on fire.

st.prompt: Which part of a candle is actually burning in the flame?

options.t: Wax that has turned into a gas
The cotton wick
Melted liquid wax

st.reveal: Heat melts the wax, the wick soaks it up, and the flame turns it into a gas. That gas is what burns. The wick only chars slowly, which is why a candle lasts for hours.

myth: The wick is the fuel that burns in a candle.
The wick is only a pump. The real fuel is wax vapour. A bare wick with no wax burns away in seconds, while a wick fed with wax can last all evening.

sec.h: Reading the colours of a flame
sec.t:
Look closely at a calm candle flame and you can see layers. Right at the bottom, near the wick, there is a small blue zone. Here the wax gas meets plenty of oxygen and burns cleanly.

Higher up, the flame turns bright yellow. Inside it, there isn't quite enough oxygen to burn everything at once. Tiny specks of carbon, called soot, form and get so hot that they glow, like the coil in an old [[@light-bulb|light bulb]]. That glow is most of a candle's light. The specks burn up before they escape, unless something disturbs the flame.

When the burning is complete, the [[combustion|combustion]] leaves behind mostly carbon dioxide and water vapour. Hold a cold steel spoon well above a flame, and an adult can show you the mist of water that forms on it.

On Earth, hot gas from a flame is lighter than the cooler air around it, so it rises. Fresh air rushes in at the bottom. That flow stretches the flame into its teardrop shape.

On the [[@space-station|International Space Station]] there is no "up" for hot gas to float towards. NASA experiments have shown that flames there become round, small and blue. Oxygen can only drift in slowly, so they burn gently and are easy to put out.

For centuries, most people made candles from tallow, which is animal fat. Tallow candles were cheap, but they smoked and smelled of cooking. Beeswax candles burned cleaner and smelled sweet, so churches and rich families used them. Bees make that wax in their hives, the same hives they guide each other to with a [[@bees-dance|waggle dance]].

In the 1850s, chemists learned to make paraffin wax from petroleum, the same [[@oil-coal|oil]] that becomes petrol. Paraffin was cheap and clean, and most candles today are still made from it. In India, many families light oil lamps called diyas for [[@diwali-lights|Diwali]], which work on the same idea: a cotton wick lifting oil to a flame.

In 1848, the scientist Michael Faraday gave a series of Christmas lectures for children in London about a single candle. They became a book that is still in print, and he explained almost everything above with nothing more than a flame and a few jars.

text: The longest tunnel on Earth is the Delaware Aqueduct, a water tunnel about 137 km long that feeds New York City. It was finished in 1945 and still supplies about half of the city's water.

For trains, the record belongs to the Gotthard Base Tunnel in Switzerland, at 57.1 km. For cars, it is the Laerdal Tunnel in Norway, at 24.5 km. And the Channel Tunnel between England and France runs about 38 km under the sea, the longest undersea stretch of any tunnel.

options.t: About 45°C, hotter than a Delhi summer afternoon
About 5°C, like a fridge
About 20°C, like a pleasant spring day

st.reveal: The deeper you go into the Earth, the warmer the rock gets. Under 2 km of mountain, the Gotthard rock reached about 45°C, so huge cooling machines had to blow chilled air at the workers.

d.try: Make a mini tunnel boring machine test. Pack damp sand firmly into a shoe box, then try to push a toilet roll tube through it sideways. Next, twist the tube as you push. The twisting tube is a tiny version of how a boring machine's spinning head cuts through rock.
myth: Long tunnels are dangerous because the air inside runs out.

sec.t:
The Delaware Aqueduct carries water from mountain reservoirs north of New York down to the city. It is about 4 m wide, big enough to drive a car through, though nobody does. Water rushes through it day and night, more than a billion litres a day.

It has also leaked for decades, losing millions of litres every day through cracks. So engineers dug a new 4 km bypass tunnel under the Hudson River to go around the worst part.

Most long tunnels today are dug by a tunnel boring machine, or TBM. The front is a spinning steel wheel studded with hard cutting discs. It grinds slowly into the rock while conveyor belts carry the broken stone backwards.

Right behind the cutter, the machine lines the new tunnel with curved concrete pieces, like fitting rings inside a giant pipe. A good day might mean 20 to 40 m of progress. In softer ground under cities, TBMs keep the soil from collapsing by pushing back against it with mud or foam.

Japan's Seikan Tunnel, 53.9 km long, links two islands under a stormy strait. It held the world record for years. The Channel Tunnel, opened in 1994, is slightly shorter at about 50 km, but more of it lies beneath the sea.

Eurostar trains pass through it in about 20 minutes, and shuttle trains carrying cars and trucks take about 35. When the two digging teams met in the middle in 1990, they were only about 36 cm apart, less than the length of a school ruler and a half.

India's own record tunnels are mostly in the Himalaya. The [[@india-wonder-atal-tunnel|Atal Tunnel]] under the Rohtang Pass, opened in 2020, is about 9 km long. It is the world's longest highway tunnel above 10,000 feet (about 3,000 m).

The railway to Kashmir, finished in 2025, needed dozens of tunnels. The longest, called T-50, runs about 12.8 km between Khari and Sumber stations. The Pir Panjal tunnel nearby is about 11.2 km. An even longer railway tunnel, about 14.5 km, has been dug in Uttarakhand for the new line to Karnaprayag, which was still being finished in 2026.

The Brenner Base Tunnel between Austria and Italy will be about 55 km long. Joined to an existing tunnel near Innsbruck, it will give trains a 64 km underground run, longer than Gotthard. It is due in the 2030s.

Engineers are also building the Fehmarnbelt Tunnel between Denmark and Germany. It is made from giant concrete pieces, each longer than two football fields, sunk into a trench on the seabed. Tunnel builders and bridge builders race each other across the same seas, and some of the [[@extreme-longest-bridges|longest bridges]] stretch even farther than these tunnels.

text: A diamond is carbon, the same stuff as the graphite in your [[@pencils|pencil]]. The difference is how the atoms are packed. In graphite, carbon atoms sit in flat sheets that slide apart. In diamond, each atom locks onto four others in a tight 3D frame, which makes it the hardest natural material known.

Natural diamonds form about 150 to 200 kilometres underground, in the [[mantle|mantle]], where it is hotter than 1,000 °C and the pressure is crushing. Rare, deep volcanic eruptions carried them up to the surface. Then miners dig them out, and cutters grind them into shapes that throw light back like fire.

st.prompt: Diamond is the hardest natural material. So what do workers use to cut and polish one?

options.t: Other diamonds, as dust on a spinning wheel, plus lasers
A very sharp steel saw
Strong acid that melts the edges

st.reveal: Only diamond can scratch diamond. Polishers press stones against wheels coated with diamond dust, and lasers do much of the sawing today. Each flat face, called a facet, is ground on at a precise angle.

d.try: Shine a torch through a glass of water, a clear marble and a piece of glass bangle in a dark room, and look at the patterns on the wall. See which one splits the light into the most colours. Diamonds are cut to bend and split light like this, but far more strongly.
myth: Diamonds are unbreakable.

Diamond is very hard, which means it is hard to scratch. But it is also brittle. A sharp knock in the wrong direction can split or chip it, which is why cutters can cleave a rough diamond with one well-aimed tap.
facts: pure carbon, the same element as pencil lead

sec.t:
Most natural diamonds are between 1 and 3.5 billion years old. They formed long before dinosaurs, before plants grew on land. Down in the mantle, the pressure is roughly 50,000 times that of the air around you, like balancing a loaded lorry on a fingernail.

Diamonds would stay there forever without a ride. Long ago, unusual eruptions blasted up from deep below and through the crust, probably rising tens of kilometres an hour. They left carrot-shaped pipes of a rock called kimberlite, named after Kimberley in South Africa. If the trip had been slow, the diamonds would have turned into graphite on the way.

sec.h: When India was the world's only source

sec.t:
A rough diamond looks like cloudy glass. Cutters plan every cut carefully, often with computer scans, to get the biggest, brightest stone with the fewest flaws. Only diamond can scratch diamond, so stones are sawn with [[@lasers|lasers]] and ground on spinning wheels coated with diamond dust.

The popular round brilliant cut has 57 or 58 flat faces called facets. In 1919, an engineer named Marcel Tolkowsky worked out angles that bounce the most light back to your eye. Light enters the top, bounces off the slanted bottom faces and comes back out split into colours.

Most of the world's diamonds pass through one Indian city. Surat in Gujarat cuts and polishes the large majority of them, often said to be around 90%, in thousands of workshops. A stone might be mined in Botswana or Russia, cut in Surat and sold in New York. The boom began in the 1960s and 70s, when Indian traders bought small, cheap rough stones that cutters elsewhere thought were not worth the work. Skilled hands made them sparkle, and the industry grew from there.

Since the 1950s, scientists have been able to make diamonds by copying the heat and pressure of the deep Earth. Newer machines grow them layer by layer from carbon-rich gas. Lab-grown diamonds have the same atoms and the same hardness as mined ones. Factories use tiny ones on drill bits and saws.

And the strangest part? Scientists think the crushing depths inside Neptune and Uranus may squeeze carbon into [[@gems-crystals|crystals]] too, so diamonds could be falling inside those planets like hail.

text: Velcro is made of two strips of fabric. One is covered in thousands of tiny stiff hooks. The other is covered in thousands of soft loops. Press them together and many hooks catch on many loops. Each hook is weak on its own, but together they hold surprisingly hard. A small strip on a shoe can easily take a day of running about. Wider strips, made of tougher plastic, can even hold pictures and tools up on walls.

To open it, you peel one strip back. That way you are only pulling a few hooks free at a time, so it is easy. The ripping sound is hundreds of hooks being dragged open, one after another. Pulling the whole strip straight apart at once is much harder, because every hook has to let go together.
The idea came from nature. In 1941, a Swiss engineer named George de Mestral noticed how burrs clung to his clothes and his dog's fur, and wondered why.

st.prompt: George de Mestral got his idea from burrs, the seed cases of the burdock plant. Why do burrs grow hooks in nature?

options.t: To catch on passing animals so the seeds travel to new places
To stop insects from eating them
To hold on to the branch in strong wind

st.reveal: Burdock seeds can't fly or float. By hooking onto fur, feathers or socks, they hitch a ride and get dropped somewhere new, where they might grow. De Mestral's dog was doing exactly the job the plant intended.

sec.t:
Copying the burr turned out to be hard. De Mestral first tried cotton, but cotton hooks were too soft and wore out quickly. Eventually he found that nylon, a new plastic fabric, could be shaped into strong, springy hooks.

Making them was the next puzzle. He worked out a way to [[@knitting-weaving|weave]] nylon into loops, toughen them with heat, and snip some of the loops so they became hooks. It took him about ten years. He received a patent in 1955 and named his invention Velcro, from the French words *velours*, meaning velvet, and *crochet*, meaning hook.

At first, [[@fashion-history|fashion]] designers weren't impressed. The fastener looked rough and cheap. Then, in the 1960s, it found a home in space. Inside a spacecraft, everything floats unless it is held down. Astronauts on the Apollo missions used patches of it to stick pens, food packets and equipment to the walls.

Astronauts on the [[@space-station|International Space Station]] still do. Some have even stuck a small patch inside their [[@spacesuits|spacesuit]] helmets to scratch an itchy nose. After the Moon missions, children's shoes, [[@life-school-bags|school bags]] and jackets began using it, and sales took off.

Velcro is a company name, so the general name for the product is hook-and-loop fastener. The company has politely asked people not to call every hook-and-loop strip "velcro", much as some people say "Xerox" for any photocopy.

De Mestral's idea is now a classic example of what scientists call biomimicry, copying designs from living things. Engineers have studied the burr alongside other natural wonders, such as [[@power-gecko-feet|gecko feet]] that cling to walls and shark skin that slips through water. Next to a [[@zippers|zip]], Velcro is one of the simplest fasteners ever made, and its hooks still look almost exactly like the burdock's.

text: Jaipur blue pottery is a glazed craft famous for its bright cobalt blue and turquoise patterns of flowers, birds and swirling vines on a white background. Unlike almost every other kind of pottery, it isn't made from ordinary potter's clay, and the only clay in it is a little Multani mitti. The dough is a mix of quartz powder, powdered glass, Multani mitti (Fuller's earth), borax and plant gum.

Artisans shape this dough in moulds, paint it by hand and fire it at low heat. The result is light, shiny and stays cool to the touch, which made it popular for water pots in hot Rajasthan. Today you will see it as vases, plates, doorknobs, tiles and tiny beads, sold in Jaipur's markets and shops around the world.

st.prompt: Jaipur blue pottery is famously fragile. Why?

options.t: It is made from quartz and glass instead of clay, and fired at a low temperature
Potters make it thin on purpose so it breaks and people buy more
The blue paint weakens it

st.reveal: Without clay to bind it, the quartz dough is hard to shape and easy to crack. It is also fired at a lower temperature than stoneware, so it never becomes as tough. That makes every piece a careful job, and many crack in the kiln.

myth: Blue pottery is an ancient art that has been made in Jaipur for thousands of years.

The technique reached India from Persia and Central Asia over several centuries, and Jaipur's workshops date mainly from the 1800s. The craft nearly vanished in the 20th century and was revived in the 1950s and 1960s.

sec.t:
First, the ingredients are ground, mixed with water and kneaded into a stiff dough. Because there is no clay, it is hard to shape on a wheel. Instead, artisans roll it flat like a roti and press it into moulds, then fill the inside with ash or sand to support it while it dries.

Once dry, pieces are smoothed, coated in a white base layer and painted with brushes made of squirrel hair or goat hair. The blue comes from cobalt oxide, and the green from copper oxide. Finally, a glassy glaze is added and the piece is fired once in a kiln at about 800 °C, much cooler than the heat used for stoneware.

By the middle of the 20th century, blue pottery had almost disappeared from Jaipur. Few artisans remained, and cheaper factory goods took over. Then the painter Kripal Singh Shekhawat, who had studied art in Shantiniketan and Japan, began working with the old techniques in the 1950s and 1960s.

He had important supporters. Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay, a freedom fighter who worked to revive Indian crafts, and Rajmata Gayatri Devi of Jaipur encouraged the effort. Shekhawat added new colours and designs and trained many younger artisans. He was awarded the Padma Shri in 1974.

The [[@glass-made|glass]] and quartz give blue pottery its glassy shine, but they also make it delicate. Without clay to stretch and bend, the dough cracks easily as it dries, and some pieces break in the kiln. Artisans expect to lose a share of every batch.

That fragility helps explain why it's handmade in small workshops, not mass-produced in big factories. Each piece is slightly different, and many carry the potter's signature.

In 2008, Blue Pottery of Jaipur received a Geographical Indication tag, which protects the name for pottery made in the Jaipur region using the traditional method. Hundreds of artisans work in and around the city, many in the Kot Jewar area and in Jaipur's old city.

Designers now mix tradition with new ideas, from fridge magnets to light fittings. Visitors to [[@jaipur|Jaipur]] can watch artisans at work in their studios. And the bright blue on every piece connects to a much older story of colour, glaze and trade stretching back to [[@ancient-persia|ancient Persia]].

text: A kolam is a pattern drawn at the doorstep, usually with rice flour, every morning across Tamil Nadu and much of South India. Many kolams start with a grid of dots, called *pulli*. The artist then draws lines around and between the dots, often as one unbroken line that loops back to where it began.

Hidden in these patterns is a lot of maths. Most kolams have [[@symmetry|symmetry]]: turn them a quarter turn, or flip them like a mirror image, and they look the same. Some can be built from a few simple rules repeated over and over, the way a computer program builds a picture.
That's why mathematicians and computer scientists have studied kolams for more than 50 years.

quiz.prompt: A kolam looks exactly the same after you turn it a quarter of the way round. How many times does it match itself in one full turn?

options.t: Four times
Two times
Eight times

quiz.reveal: A full turn is four quarter turns, so the pattern matches itself four times. Mathematicians call this rotational symmetry of order four. A plus sign has it too.

Then stand a small mirror across the middle of your pattern. If the half you see plus its reflection looks like the whole, your kolam has mirror symmetry.
myth: Kolams are only drawn for festivals.
In many South Indian homes, a fresh kolam is drawn at the doorstep every morning. Festivals bring bigger and more colourful ones, but the daily kolam is the heart of the tradition.

sec.t:
Different parts of India have their own floor art. In Tamil Nadu it's kolam, in Andhra Pradesh and Telangana muggu, in Bengal alpana and in Rajasthan mandana. [[@rangoli-art|Rangoli]] is the name used in Maharashtra, Gujarat and much of the north, often with bright coloured powders at festivals such as [[@diwali-lights|Diwali]]. In [[@kerala|Kerala]], during Onam, families make the *pookalam*, a circle of fresh flower petals.

The daily kolam is usually white and drawn fresh at dawn, after the doorstep is swept and sprinkled with water. During the Tamil month of Margazhi, from mid-December to mid-January, kolams grow huge and competitive, sometimes filling whole streets. At [[@onam-pongal|Pongal]], they often show pots of boiling rice, sugarcane and the sun.

sec.h: The maths of dots and loops

sec.t:
In the 1970s, Gift Siromoney, a mathematician at Madras Christian College in [[@chennai|Chennai]], began studying kolams with his colleagues. They showed that kolam patterns could be described with "array grammars": sets of rules a computer can follow to build a picture step by step. A few simple rules can produce surprisingly complicated designs.

Later, the American mathematician Marcia Ascher wrote about the kolam as a living tradition of mathematical thinking. Computer scientists have since written programs that draw kolams, and designers borrow them for fabrics and floor [[@tessellations|tiles]].

Traditional kolams are drawn with rice flour, and that choice is no accident. By midday, ants, birds and other small creatures have often eaten parts of the pattern. Many families see this as a small daily act of feeding other living things.

The kolam is also meant to be temporary. Feet, wind and rain wipe it away, and the next morning it is drawn again. Children often learn by watching mothers and grandmothers, practising until their fingers can let the flour fall in a thin, steady line. Today people of all ages draw them, from village lanes in Thanjavur to apartment doorways in New Jersey.

text: Amul is owned by dairy farmers in Gujarat. It began in 1946 in the town of Anand, in what was then Kaira district, as a way for farmers to stop being cheated by a private dairy.

The farmers formed village milk societies. Each morning and evening, they brought their milk to a village collection centre, where it was tested and paid for fairly. The societies joined together into a district union, which processed the milk and sold it. Over time, unions across Gujarat joined to sell under one brand name, Amul. Today the system has lakhs of farmer members, many of them women with only one or two buffaloes.

sec.t:
In 1949, a young engineer named Verghese Kurien was posted to a government dairy in Anand. He wanted to leave. Instead, Tribhuvandas Patel persuaded him to help the struggling cooperative, and he stayed for the rest of his working life.

Kurien, along with engineer H. M. Dalaya, solved a big problem. Most of Kaira's milk came from buffaloes, and experts said buffalo milk couldn't be dried into powder. Dalaya found a way, and in 1955 a new plant began making milk powder and butter. The brand name Amul came from the Sanskrit word *amulya*, meaning priceless.

Prime Minister [[@lal-bahadur-shastri|Lal Bahadur Shastri]] visited Anand in 1964 and asked Kurien to copy the model across India. The National Dairy Development Board was set up in 1965, and in 1970 it launched Operation Flood. Milk unions on the Anand pattern were started in hundreds of districts, linked to cities by refrigerated road and rail tankers.

This came to be called the [[@white-revolution|White Revolution]]. India became the world's largest milk producer in the late 1990s and has stayed there since. In Gujarat, the district unions formed a joint federation in 1973 to sell everything under the Amul name, from milk and butter to [[@ice-cream-freezing|ice cream]] and chocolate. Kurien's birthday, 26 November, is now marked as National Milk Day.

sec.h: The girl in the polka-dot dress
sec.t:
Since 1966, Amul's adverts have starred a chubby little girl in a polka-dot dress, created by the advertising agency of Sylvester daCunha. Her billboards make jokes about the news of the week, often with [[@words-puns|puns]]. The slogan "Utterly Butterly Delicious" has run for decades.

The ads are famous, but the bigger story is behind them. A farmer in a Gujarat village who brings a few litres of [[@milk|milk]] to the local society each morning is a part-owner of the whole business. In 1976, about five lakh of these farmers each paid ₹2 to fund *Manthan*, a film about their own movement.

text: The "Waterman of India" is Rajendra Singh, who has spent about 40 years helping villages in Rajasthan catch rainwater. With his organisation, Tarun Bharat Sangh, he and the villagers revived old ways of building small mud dams called johads.

The johads caught monsoon rain and let it soak into the ground. Wells that had dried up filled again. Farmers could grow crops once more. And a few small rivers in Alwar district, including the Arvari, began flowing again after years of being dry for most of the year. In 2015 he won the Stockholm Water Prize, sometimes described as the Nobel Prize for water.

st.prompt: A johad holds rainwater in a pond for a few months. What is the most important thing it does?

options.t: Lets water soak slowly into the ground and refill wells
Gives people a place to swim
Keeps the water cold for drinking

st.reveal: Most of a johad's value is underground. As the pond water seeps down, it refills the groundwater, so wells nearby stop drying up. Over years, enough johads can raise the water table across a whole valley.

sec.t:
Alwar is in eastern Rajasthan, on the rocky Aravalli hills. Rain comes mostly in the monsoon months, and some years hardly at all. For centuries, villages there stored water in johads and ponds.

By the 1980s, many of these had broken or silted up. Forests on the hills had been cut, so rain rushed off the bare slopes instead of sinking in. Wells went dry. Young men left to look for work in cities. Women walked for hours to fetch water.

sec.h: A doctor who picked up a shovel

sec.t:
A johad is a curved wall of earth and stones built across a slope or a seasonal stream. It is usually no taller than a grown-up. During the monsoon, it traps the water that would have rushed away.

Some water is used directly by animals and farmers. Most of it slowly seeps down into the [[@groundwater|groundwater]], like water into a sponge. A single johad helps a few wells. Hundreds of them, spread across a valley, can lift the water level for an entire area.

Villagers did the work themselves, giving land, money and labour. Tarun Bharat Sangh says thousands of johads have been built or repaired across Rajasthan and nearby states.

The Arvari river had flowed only during the rains for years. As johads multiplied along its catchment, the area of land that drains into it, the groundwater rose. By the 1990s, the river was flowing for much more of the year.

Tarun Bharat Sangh says several other small rivers in the area, such as the Ruparel and Sarsa, have revived too. Tigers and other animals in the nearby Sariska Tiger Reserve also gained from the extra water.

When fishing contractors arrived to make money from the river, the villagers objected. They formed the Arvari River Parliament, where representatives from dozens of villages make rules for using the river fairly.

Singh has walked across India to talk about water, and has worked in other countries facing droughts. He argues that water belongs to communities, and that old Indian knowledge, from village ponds to grand [[@stepwells|stepwells]], still has lessons for today.

His story sits alongside other Indians who changed their land with their own hands. In Bihar, a labourer known as the [[@india-mountain-man|Mountain Man]] spent 22 years cutting a path through a rocky ridge with a hammer and chisel.

text: Umpires and referees are the people who apply the rules in a game. In cricket, tennis and baseball they are usually called umpires. In football, basketball and hockey they are referees. Either way, their job is to see what happened, decide in a split second, and stick to the decision while thousands of people shout at them.

To get there, officials study thick rulebooks, pass exams, stay fit and work their way up from school and local matches. Top football referees train like athletes. Top cricket umpires stand for six or seven hours a day, focusing on every ball. Most have one thing in common: they love a sport but never played it at the very highest level.

They are very accurate, but they still estimate where the ball would have gone, with a small margin of error of a few millimetres. That is why cricket's review system has "umpire's call", which keeps the on-field decision when the replay is too close to be sure.

sec.t:
Every sport has its rulebook. Cricket's Laws have been looked after by the Marylebone Cricket Club in London since 1788. Football's Laws of the Game are set by the International Football Association Board, formed in 1886. Officials must know these rules well enough to apply them without thinking, from the tricky [[@cricket-rules|leg before wicket]] law in cricket to [[@football-rules|offside]] in football. The rulebooks change too, so officials have to keep relearning them.

New umpires and referees take courses and written tests. In India, cricket umpires climb through state and national exams before they officiate in big matches. Referees are watched and graded after games, and the best are promoted. A single mistake in a big match can follow them for years.

Football referees need to keep up with play. In a top match, a referee often runs more than 10 km, with lots of short sprints. They take regular fitness tests, and many train with sports scientists.

Cricket umpires need a different kind of stamina. They stand in sun or cold for a whole day, judging whether a ball would have hit the stumps or brushed the bat. Calm matters just as much. Officials learn to explain decisions clearly and to stay steady when players, coaches and crowds disagree.

sec.h: Signals the whole ground can read
sec.t:
Officials speak with their hands as much as their voices. A cricket umpire raises one finger for out and lifts both arms high for a six. A football referee points to the spot for a penalty. In baseball, the home plate umpire calls a strike with a sharp punch or point of the right arm, so even fans in the farthest seats can follow.

Football's coloured cards came from a moment at a traffic light. At the 1966 World Cup, there was confusion about which players had been warned. Afterwards, English referee Ken Aston, stopped at a [[@traffic-lights|traffic light]] in London, realised that colours speak every language. Yellow and red cards were first used at the 1970 World Cup in Mexico.

text: The Super Bowl is the championship game of the National Football League (NFL), the top American football league. It is played on a Sunday in early February and is the most-watched television broadcast in the USA most years. In 2025, about 128 million Americans watched.

It is big for more reasons than the football. There is a huge halftime music show, famous adverts that cost millions of dollars, and parties with mountains of snacks. For many families, Super Bowl Sunday is almost a holiday.

sec.t:
In the 1960s there were two rival professional football leagues, the NFL and the newer American Football League (AFL). They agreed to merge, and from 1967 their champions met in a final game.

The first game, on 15 January 1967, was called the AFL-NFL World Championship Game. The Green Bay Packers beat the Kansas City Chiefs 35–10 at the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum, and thousands of seats were empty. Lamar Hunt, who owned the Chiefs, had joked about calling it the "Super Bowl" after his children's Super Ball toy. The name caught on.

The game is now played in a different city each year, chosen years in advance. Warm places like Miami, New Orleans and Los Angeles, and cities with [[@stadiums|roofed stadiums]], are favourites, because February can be freezing in much of the USA. Cities compete to host it, hoping for millions of dollars from visitors.

Because so many people watch, companies pay huge sums for advertising time. In 2025, a 30-second slot cost around 8 million US dollars. Brands try to make funny, surprising or emotional adverts, and people discuss them at school and work the next day.

Some adverts became famous on their own. In 1984 Apple showed a cinema-style advert for its new Macintosh computer, and people still talk about it. Today many companies release their Super Bowl adverts online before the game.

At halftime, a major music star performs a short, spectacular show on a stage built in minutes on the field. [[@michael-jackson|Michael Jackson]]'s show in 1993 helped make halftime a must-watch event. Since then, singers from Beyoncé to Rihanna have performed.

Performers are not paid their usual concert fees, but the exposure is enormous. For some viewers the halftime show is the main event. Others watch only for the game and the famous last-minute finishes.

Americans eat huge amounts of food on Super Bowl Sunday. The National Chicken Council estimates that well over a billion chicken wings are eaten around the game. Host cities, such as [[@new-orleans|New Orleans]] in 2025, fill their hotels and restaurants.

India's biggest cricket matches attract even larger audiences. An India–Pakistan World Cup game or an [[@ipl|IPL]] final can draw hundreds of millions of viewers on TV and streaming. The Super Bowl is unusual because almost all of its audience is in one country, watching together on one evening.

text: Apps are programs, so they are made from code. But code is only one part. Most apps go through a series of stages.

It begins with an idea: a problem someone wants to solve, like ordering food, learning words or paying a friend. Designers sketch how the app should look and work. Programmers write the code. Testers try to break it. Then it is sent to an app store, checked, and released. After that, the work carries on, with updates to fix problems and add features.
A simple app might be built by one person in weeks. A big app like a bank's or a game may need hundreds of people and years.

st.prompt: Many apps are free to download. How do most free apps earn money?

options.t: Through adverts, paid extras inside the app, or subscriptions
The government pays for them

st.reveal: Building and running an app costs money for programmers, designers and servers. Free apps often show adverts, sell extra features or levels, or offer a paid version. Some use information about how people use the app to target adverts.

Give it to a friend, and as they "tap" with a finger, swap the drawings. Watch where they get confused and redraw. Designers call this a paper prototype.
myth: Free apps cost nothing to make.
Even simple apps take many hours of design, coding and testing, and popular apps pay for servers and staff every day. Free apps usually earn money in other ways, such as adverts or paid upgrades.

sec.t:
An app usually has two halves. The front end is what you see and touch on your [[@smartphones|phone]]: the screens, buttons and animations. It is often written in languages like Swift for iPhones or Kotlin for Android phones.

The back end runs on computers called [[server|servers]], far away in [[@data-centres|data centres]]. It stores accounts, messages and photos, and does heavy work your phone can't. Much of this now runs in [[@cloud-computing|the cloud]], on servers rented from big companies. The two halves talk to each other over the [[@internet-how|internet]].

Programmers use ready-made building blocks for common jobs, such as maps, logins and payments, so they don't have to write everything from scratch.

Every app has bugs at first. Testers try it on old phones and new ones, on slow internet and fast, in different languages and with unusual inputs. Some companies give early versions to volunteers, called beta testers, before the public sees them.

Programmers also write automatic tests: small programs that check the main program still works each time someone changes it. A popular app might run thousands of these tests a day.

Apple's App Store and Google's store for Android, then called Android Market, both opened in 2008. Today they hold millions of apps. Before an app goes live, the store checks it against rules about safety, [[@privacy|privacy]] and content.

Apps also need permission to use things like your camera, microphone or location. Those pop-up questions on your phone exist so you can decide what each app can access. It is worth reading them.

Some apps have changed daily life. India's [[@upi-payments|UPI payment system]], launched in 2016, lets people pay with apps by scanning a QR code, and it now handles billions of payments a month, from big shops to tea stalls. [[@digital-india|Government apps such as DigiLocker]] let people keep official documents on their phones.

You don't need to be a professional to start. Free tools like MIT App Inventor let beginners build simple Android apps by snapping blocks together. Many developers who now work on famous apps began by building something small for themselves.

text: Most submarines have to come up regularly, because their diesel engines need air and their batteries need charging. Nuclear submarines are different. Their reactor makes heat without burning anything, so it needs no air. A single load of fuel can last many years.

With power to spare, a nuclear submarine makes everything else it needs. Machines turn seawater into fresh water. Other machines split water to make oxygen. Chemical filters soak up the carbon dioxide the crew breathes out.

So in theory it could stay down for years. In practice, patrols usually last two or three months. The limit is people: their food, their health and how long they can live in a steel tube without sunlight.

st.prompt: How does a submarine sink on purpose, then rise again?

options.t: By letting seawater into tanks, then blowing it out with compressed air
By switching its engine to spin backwards
By dropping heavy anchors, then pulling them up

st.reveal: Ballast tanks fill with water to make the submarine heavier so it sinks. To rise, compressed air forces the water out, making the sub lighter than the water it displaces.

d.try: Make a mini submarine with an empty plastic bottle and a flexible straw. Fill the bottle with water in a sink, push the straw in, and seal around it with modelling clay. Blow gently through the straw to push water out and watch the bottle float up, then let water back in to make it sink. That's how ballast tanks work.
myth: Military submarines can dive to the very bottom of the ocean.

Most military submarines work at depths of a few hundred metres. The deepest parts of the ocean are about 11 km down, and only special craft built for that one job, like the bathyscaphe Trieste in 1960, have reached them.
