sec.t:
A submarine has ballast tanks between its inner and outer hulls. To dive, valves open and seawater floods in. The sub gets heavier and sinks. Small fins called hydroplanes tilt it up or down, like the wings of an aircraft.

To rise, the crew blows high-pressure air into the tanks, pushing the water out. The sub gets lighter and floats up. This is all about [[buoyancy|buoyancy]]: an object floats when it weighs less than the water it pushes aside.

The inner hull, called the pressure hull, is made of thick, strong steel. At 300 metres down, the water presses on every square centimetre about 30 times harder than air does at the surface.

Air is the first problem. A crew of about 100 to 150 people uses a lot of oxygen. Nuclear submarines run electricity through water, splitting it into oxygen, which goes into the air, and hydrogen, which is pumped overboard. Scrubbers soak up carbon dioxide. Backup "oxygen candles" can release oxygen in an emergency.

Water comes from the sea. Distilling machines boil seawater and collect the steam, leaving salt behind, much as people [[@water-purify|purify water]] on land. Some of the water cools the reactor, and the rest goes to drinking, cooking and showers.

The world's first nuclear-powered submarine, the US Navy's USS *Nautilus*, was launched in 1954. It shared its name with Captain Nemo's submarine in a novel by [[@jules-verne|Jules Verne]]. In August 1958, it travelled under the Arctic ice and became the first vessel to pass beneath the North Pole.

Today, only a few countries operate nuclear submarines. India joined them with INS *Arihant*, its first home-built nuclear submarine, which was commissioned in 2016. India also runs diesel-electric submarines like INS *Kalvari*.

Crews live by the clock, not the sun. Many submarines run on shifts, so there's always someone awake. Bunks are narrow, and in some subs sailors share beds in turns, called "hot racking". Food is planned carefully: fresh fruit and milk run out first, then frozen and tinned food takes over.

Sailors keep fit on exercise machines, watch films and study. Many say the hardest part isn't the danger but missing the sky. When a submarine surfaces after a long patrol, the first breath of real air is something crews talk about for years.

text: Carthage was a city on the coast of North Africa, in what is now Tunisia. It was started by sailors from Tyre, a port in today's Lebanon, traditionally in 814 BCE. These sailors were [[@phoenicians|Phoenicians]], famous traders who carried goods all around the Mediterranean Sea.
Carthage grew rich and powerful. Its ships sailed to Spain, Sicily and beyond, and it ruled a trading empire for hundreds of years.
Then it ran into another rising power across the sea: [[@ancient-rome|Rome]]. The two fought three long wars, called the Punic Wars. In 146 BCE the Romans captured Carthage and burned it.

st.prompt: After Rome destroyed Carthage in 146 BCE, what happened to the site?

options.t: The Romans later built a new city of their own there
It was salted so nothing could ever grow again
It was left empty until modern times

st.reveal: About a hundred years later Julius Caesar and then Augustus started a Roman Carthage on the same spot. It became one of the biggest cities in Roman Africa. The salting story was invented much later.

src: Britannica, "Carthage" and "Punic Wars".
UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Archaeological Site of Carthage.
Richard Miles, Carthage Must Be Destroyed (2010).
n.certNote: Most of what we know about Carthage was written by its enemies, the Greeks and Romans, because Carthage's own books were lost. Its founding date of 814 BCE comes from tradition, though archaeology shows a town there by the 700s BCE.

myth: The Romans ploughed salt into the ground at Carthage so that nothing would grow there again.

No ancient writer says this. The story seems to have appeared about two thousand years later, in the 1800s and 1900s. The Romans did burn the city, but they soon farmed the land around it and later rebuilt the city itself.

sec.h: A city built on a story
sec.t:
Romans told a famous legend about how it began. A princess named Elissa, also called Dido, fled Tyre and landed in Africa. A local king said she could have as much land as an ox hide could cover.

Elissa cut the hide into very thin strips and laid them end to end around a whole hill. That hill, the Byrsa, became the heart of Carthage.

Nobody knows if any of this happened. What archaeologists can say is that people were living at Carthage by the 700s BCE, which fits the old tradition quite well.

The most famous Carthaginian is a general named Hannibal. In 218 BCE, during the Second Punic War, he marched an army from Spain, over the Pyrenees and then across the snowy Alps into Italy. He brought war elephants with him.

Many soldiers and most of the elephants died on the way. Even so, Hannibal beat the Romans in battle after battle. At Cannae in 216 BCE he surrounded and crushed a much larger Roman army.

Which elephants did he use? Historians think most were a smaller kind of African elephant that once lived in North Africa and has since died out there. A Roman writer says Hannibal's bravest elephant was called Surus, which may mean "the Syrian", so it might have been an Asian elephant.

He never captured Rome itself, though. The Romans sent an army to attack Carthage, and Hannibal had to hurry home. In 202 BCE a Roman general named Scipio defeated him at Zama.

Carthage lost its empire but kept trading and grew wealthy again. Some Romans could not stand that. A senator called Cato the Elder was said to end his speeches with the words "Carthage must be destroyed."

In 149 BCE Rome attacked. After a siege of about three years, the city fell in 146 BCE. Most of the survivors were sold into slavery.

The story did not end there. Roughly a hundred years later the Romans built a new Carthage on the same spot, and it became one of the largest cities in Roman Africa. Its ruins now sit among the houses of a seaside suburb of Tunis, where [[@archaeology|archaeologists]] still dig.

text: Pokhran is a small town in the Thar Desert of Rajasthan, near the army's Pokhran test range. India has carried out nuclear tests there twice. On 18 May 1974, it exploded one nuclear device underground. On 11 and 13 May 1998, it tested five more.

After the 1998 tests, India declared itself a nuclear weapons state. Two weeks later, Pakistan carried out its own tests. Many countries condemned India and Pakistan, and some placed sanctions on them. The tests remain a source of national pride for many Indians, and a subject of worry and argument for others.

st.prompt: How did India keep the 1998 tests secret from spy satellites?

options.t: Workers moved mostly at night and covered their tracks and equipment
They held the tests on a cloudy day
They built the test site underground in a city

st.reveal: The team worked in the dark hours, dressed in army uniforms, put equipment back in the same place every morning and filled shafts under camouflage nets. The US was caught by surprise.

n.certNote: The dates and basic facts of the tests are well recorded. The exact power of the 1998 explosions is still debated, and people disagree strongly about whether nuclear weapons make countries safer.

sec.t:
India's nuclear programme began in the 1940s under the physicist [[@homi-bhabha|Homi Bhabha]]. At first it focused on [[@nuclear-power|nuclear power]] and research. But India had fought a war with China in 1962, and China tested its first nuclear bomb in 1964. Many Indian leaders felt the country could not be left behind.

India also argued that the world's nuclear rules were unfair. The Non-Proliferation Treaty of 1968 allowed five countries, including the US, the Soviet Union and China, to keep nuclear weapons while asking everyone else to give them up. India refused to sign it, and still has not.

In 1998, Prime Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee's government approved new tests. The effort was led by [[@apj-kalam|A. P. J. Abdul Kalam]], then head of the Defence Research and Development Organisation, and R. Chidambaram of the Department of Atomic Energy.

India knew American satellites were watching. In 1995, a planned test had been called off after US satellites spotted signs of preparation. This time, the team worked mostly at night, shifted equipment back into the same position by daylight, and wore army uniforms. Some scientists used false names.

At 3:45 in the afternoon on 11 May 1998, three devices went off together. Two smaller ones followed on 13 May. India's government said the largest was a thermonuclear, or hydrogen, device. Some scientists in India and abroad have questioned how powerful it really was.

The reaction came quickly. The US, Japan and other countries put sanctions on India, cutting aid and loans. The UN Security Council condemned the tests. On 28 and 30 May, Pakistan tested its own devices in the Chagai Hills.

India then announced a voluntary stop on further testing and a "no first use" policy, meaning it says it will not be the first to use nuclear weapons in a conflict. Over the next decade, relations with the US improved, and in 2008 the two countries signed a deal allowing India to buy fuel for its nuclear power plants.

The test range is still a closed military area in the [[@thar-formed|Thar Desert]]. The town of Pokhran itself is much older than the tests, with a 14th-century sandstone fort called Balagarh, built when camel caravans crossed this part of the desert. People in nearby villages remember the ground shaking and walls cracking in 1998. In 2018, a Bollywood film about the tests renewed public interest.

India marks 11 May every year as National Technology Day, to honour science and engineering, not just the bombs.

text: Alaska is the biggest US state, more than twice the size of Texas, but very few people live there, about 740,000. It sits in the far north-west of North America, next to [[@canada|Canada]], with Russia just across the sea. Much of it is wilderness: mountains, glaciers, forests and [[@tundra|tundra]], which is cold, treeless land with frozen soil underneath.

Life in Alaska follows the seasons. Summer days are very long, and people fish, hike and work outdoors late into the bright evening. Winters are long, dark and cold. In many villages there are no roads at all, and people travel by small plane, boat or snowmobile.

d.try: Model the midnight Sun. In a dark room, shine a torch at a globe or a ball (the Sun). Tilt the top of the ball towards the torch and slowly spin it. Watch a sticker placed near the top. It stays in the light all the way round. Now tilt the top away and see what happens.
myth: Alaska is covered in snow and ice all year.
Summers can be warm. Fairbanks sometimes passes 30 °C, and the south-east coast is covered in rainforest. Long summer days help farmers there grow very large cabbages and pumpkins.

sec.t:
Alaska Native peoples have lived there for thousands of years. They include the Iñupiat, Yupik, Unangan (Aleut), Athabascan, Tlingit and Haida. Russian fur traders arrived in the 1700s. In 1867, Russia sold Alaska to the United States for 7.2 million dollars, about two cents an acre. Some newspapers called it "Seward's Folly", after the US official who arranged the deal.

It turned out to be a bargain. Gold was found in the 1890s, and later oil. Alaska became the 49th state in 1959.

Denali, about 6,190 m tall, is the highest mountain in North America. Huge [[@glaciers|glaciers]] flow down from the mountains, and some reach the sea, where chunks of ice crash into the water. Alaska also has dozens of active [[@volcano|volcanoes]].

Alaska gets more [[@earthquakes|earthquakes]] than any other state. On 27 March 1964, a magnitude 9.2 earthquake struck, the most powerful ever recorded in North America. It shook the ground for about four and a half minutes and caused a tsunami.

sec.h: Dogs and the race to Nome
sec.t:
In 1925, a disease called diphtheria broke out in the town of Nome. Medicine was needed fast, but no plane could fly in the winter storms. Teams of sled [[@dogs-domestic|dogs]] carried it about 1,000 km in relay in under six days. The dogs Balto and Togo became famous.

Today the Iditarod sled dog race, about 1,600 km long, follows parts of that old trail every March. Mushers, the people who drive the sleds, race through blizzards with teams of 12 to 16 dogs.

In 1968, a huge oilfield was found at Prudhoe Bay on the Arctic coast. A pipeline about 1,290 km long was built to carry the [[@oil-coal|oil]] south to a port. It was finished in 1977. Oil money helps pay for schools and roads, and each year most Alaskans receive a share in a payment from an oil fund.

Alaska is also full of wildlife. Brown bears catch salmon in rivers, moose wander into towns, and whales feed off the coast. Many Alaskans hunt and fish for much of their food, as their families have for generations.

text: Bhutan is a small kingdom in the eastern Himalaya, between India and China, with fewer than 8 lakh people. Most countries judge their progress by GDP, the total value of everything they produce. In the 1970s, Bhutan's young fourth king, Jigme Singye Wangchuck, said that Gross National [[@happiness|Happiness]] was more important than Gross National Product.

The idea is that a good country helps people live good lives, which is more than simply richer ones. So Bhutan regularly asks its citizens about their health, sleep, education, community, culture, environment and how they feel. Government plans are supposed to be checked against how they affect this happiness. It doesn't make Bhutan a paradise, but it does make the country think differently about what progress means.

st.prompt: In 1999, Bhutan became one of the last countries in the world to allow something most of us take for granted. What was it?

options.t: Television and the internet
Cars

st.reveal: Bhutan's rulers worried that TV might wash away local culture, so it was kept out until 1999. That year, television and the internet were both allowed in. Today most homes in towns have a TV and a phone.

n.certNote: Bhutan really does measure Gross National Happiness and uses it in planning. Whether this has made people happier than elsewhere is debated, and critics point to poverty and the treatment of a Nepali-speaking minority.

d.try: Make a happiness survey for your class. Ask five simple questions, such as how well people slept, whether they spent time outdoors and whether they felt they had a friend to talk to. Add up the answers, and think about which ones money could change and which it couldn't.
myth: Bhutan is the happiest country in the world.
Bhutan invented the idea of Gross National Happiness, but that does not mean it tops world rankings. In international surveys of how satisfied people feel, it usually does not come near the top.

sec.t:
About 70 percent of Bhutan is covered in forest, and its constitution says that at least 60 percent must stay forested forever. All those trees absorb more carbon dioxide than the country releases, so Bhutan is often described as carbon negative, a rare thing in a world worried about [[@climate-change|climate change]].

Fast rivers rush down from the mountains, and Bhutan builds [[@dams-power|dams]] to turn them into electricity. Much of that power is sold to India, and it is the country's biggest export. Indian visitors can enter with a voter ID card instead of a passport, and the Indian rupee is accepted alongside Bhutan's own currency, the ngultrum.

Bhutan kept the outside world at arm's length for a long time. [[@television-invented|Television]] and the internet were only allowed in 1999. Climbing mountains above 6,000 metres is banned, out of respect for the gods believed to live on them. So Gangkhar Puensum, at about 7,570 metres, may be the highest mountain on Earth that nobody has climbed.

Thimphu is one of the very few capital cities with no [[@road-safety|traffic lights]]. A set was put up at a busy crossing in the 1990s, but people found it impersonal and it was soon taken down. A police officer in white gloves still waves the cars through by hand from a little painted booth.

High above the Paro valley, the Tiger's Nest monastery clings to a sheer cliff. Legend says the Buddhist teacher Guru Rinpoche flew there on the back of a tigress in the 8th century to [[@mindfulness|meditate]] in a cave.

In 2008, Bhutan held its first national elections for a parliament. The push came from the kings themselves, even though many Bhutanese wanted them to keep their power. The country's national sport is [[@archery|archery]], and village matches come with singing, dancing and cheeky teasing of the other team.

Bhutan has critics too. In the early 1990s, more than a lakh Nepali-speaking people, called Lhotshampa, left or were forced out of southern Bhutan after new rules on citizenship and dress. Many lived for years in refugee camps in Nepal, and most were later resettled in countries such as the USA. Others point out that many Bhutanese, especially in villages, are still poor, and that in recent years thousands of young people have moved abroad, many to Australia, to study and work.

text: Kyoto is a city in western Japan, ringed by green hills. It was Japan's capital and the home of its emperors from 794 until 1868, which is longer than the United States has existed, four times over. During those centuries it became the centre of Japanese art, religion, poetry and fine crafts.

Today it is a modern city of about 14 lakh people, with trains and offices. But it still has around 1,600 Buddhist temples and 400 Shinto shrines, along with old wooden houses, Zen gardens and teahouses. Seventeen of its temples, shrines and castles are together a UNESCO World Heritage Site. People come for the cherry blossoms in spring, red maple leaves in autumn, and a feeling of stepping back into old Japan.

It was too cloudy to find

st.reveal: Henry Stimson, the US Secretary of War, had visited Kyoto years before. He argued that destroying Japan's old cultural capital would be wrong and would make post-war peace harder, and he had it taken off the list.

d.try: Kyoto was laid out on a neat grid, copied from an old Chinese capital. Draw a grid of streets on squared paper, number the north–south streets and name the east–west ones. Then write directions to a friend's "house" using only the street names, the way Kyoto addresses still work.
myth: Tokyo has always been Japan's capital.
Kyoto was the emperor's home for over a thousand years. Only in 1868–69 did the young Emperor Meiji move to Edo, which was renamed Tokyo, meaning "eastern capital".
facts: about 1,600 Buddhist temples and 400 Shinto shrines

sec.t:
When the emperor moved the capital here in 794, the new city was called Heian-kyō, meaning "capital of peace and tranquillity". Its planners copied Chang'an, the great capital of Tang China, laying out straight streets in a chessboard grid with the palace at the north.

That grid still shapes Kyoto's centre, and addresses are often given as directions: go up (north) or down (south) from a crossing. Around the year 1000, a court lady named Murasaki Shikibu wrote *The Tale of Genji* here, about life among the nobles. It is often called one of the world's first novels.

Kinkaku-ji, the Golden Pavilion, is covered in real gold leaf and reflected in a still pond. In 1950 a young monk set fire to it and it burned down. It was rebuilt in 1955, as close as possible to the old one.

At Fushimi Inari shrine, thousands of bright orange torii gates line paths that climb a whole mountain. Each gate was given by a person or business, with their name painted on it. On the western edge of the city, the paths of the Arashiyama grove run between stems of [[@bamboo|bamboo]] many metres tall that creak and click in the wind.

sec.h: Cards, games and a climate treaty
sec.t:
In 1889, a craftsman named Fusajiro Yamauchi started a small business in Kyoto making hanafuda, Japanese [[@cards-games|playing cards]] decorated with flowers. The company was called [[@pokemon|Nintendo]]. Many decades later it turned to toys and then to [[@tech-game-consoles|video games]], and Mario, Zelda and the Nintendo Switch were born. Nintendo still has its headquarters in Kyoto.

In 1997, countries from around the world met in Kyoto and signed the Kyoto Protocol, one of the first big international agreements to cut the gases that cause [[@climate-change|climate change]]. So the name of an old imperial city is known by scientists and diplomats everywhere.

In the old Gion district, you may glimpse a young woman in a bright kimono and white make-up walking quickly to an appointment. In Kyoto, geisha are called geiko, and their trainees are called maiko. They spend years learning dance, music and the art of conversation.

text: Punjab is a state in north-west India, famous for its farms, its food, its music and as the home of Sikhism. Its name comes from Persian: *panj* means five and *aab* means water. The five rivers that gave it the name are the Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas and Sutlej.

Those rivers spread rich soil over a flat, wide plain. Today Punjab grows enormous amounts of wheat and rice. It is also known for the Golden Temple in [[@amritsar|Amritsar]], for loud, joyful bhangra music, and for buttery parathas and lassi. And it is known for the many Punjabis who have moved abroad, from Canada and Britain to California.

st.reveal: When Punjab was divided in 1947, most of the old province and three of its rivers went to Pakistan. Indian Punjab today has the Sutlej and the Beas, and part of the Ravi along its border.

myth: All Punjabis are Sikh.
Punjab is the home of Sikhism, and most people in Indian Punjab are Sikh. But many Punjabis are Hindu, Muslim or Christian. Across the border in Pakistani Punjab, most people are Muslim.

sec.t:
For most of history, Punjab was one region that stretched across what is now India and Pakistan. In 1947, when British rule ended, it was divided. The western part, with the city of Lahore, went to Pakistan. The eastern part stayed in India.

[[@partition|Partition]] forced millions of people to leave their homes and cross the new border, and many lost their lives in the violence. Families still tell stories of the villages they left behind. Indian Punjab was later divided again, in 1966, when Haryana and parts of Himachal Pradesh became separate. Its capital is [[@chandigarh|Chandigarh]], a planned city it shares with Haryana. The city was designed in the 1950s by the Swiss-French architect Le Corbusier, with numbered sectors laid out like squares on a chessboard.

[[@guru-nanak|Guru Nanak]], the founder of Sikhism, was born in 1469 in a village now called Nankana Sahib, in Pakistani Punjab. He taught that there is one God, that all people are equal, and that honest work and sharing matter. Nine Gurus followed him. The tenth, Guru Gobind Singh, founded the Khalsa, the community of initiated Sikhs, at Anandpur Sahib in Punjab in 1699. Their teachings are collected in the [[@guru-granth-sahib|Guru Granth Sahib]], the holy book of Sikhs.

Gurdwaras across Punjab, and across the world, run free [[@maths-recipes-scale|community kitchens]] called langar. Anyone can sit on the floor and eat, whoever they are. The Punjabi language is written in Gurmukhi, a script shaped by the Sikh Gurus, and it is the main language of the state.

Bhangra began as a harvest dance, performed by farmers celebrating the wheat crop around Baisakhi in April. With its booming dhol drum, it now fills wedding halls from Ludhiana to London. Lohri, in January, is celebrated with bonfires, songs and peanuts.

[[@punjabi-food|Punjabi food]] is hearty: sarson da saag with makki di roti, chole, and thick glasses of lassi. Much of what restaurants abroad sell as "Indian food" is really Punjabi, carried there by the people who moved overseas. Punjab's farm kitchens have travelled further than most.

text: Cape Town is squeezed between a mountain and the sea. In the middle of the city stands Table Mountain, about 1,085 m tall and almost perfectly flat on top. Around it lie white beaches, green vineyards, colourful houses and two oceans close by.

The view is only the start. The mountain is covered in plants found nowhere else, penguins waddle on a town beach, and whales swim in the bay. All of this sits in a city of about 48 lakh people (2022 census) at the south-western tip of Africa.

sec.h: A mountain older than the Himalayas
sec.t:
Table Mountain's flat top is made of tough sandstone laid down at the bottom of an ancient sea, hundreds of millions of years ago. Wind and rain wore away the softer rock around it. The [[@himalaya-form|Himalayas]], by comparison, began rising only about 50 million years ago, so Table Mountain is several times older.

When a strong south-east wind blows, moist air is pushed up over the mountain and cools into cloud. The cloud spills over the edge and melts away as it sinks. Locals call it the tablecloth. A cable car has carried visitors to the top since 1929, and its modern cars spin slowly as they rise, so every passenger gets the full view.

sec.h: A whole plant kingdom in one corner

sec.t:
At Boulders Beach, a short drive from the city, African penguins nest among big granite rocks. Swimmers sometimes share the water with them. Only two pairs settled there in 1982. The colony grew to thousands, but African penguins have declined so sharply across their range that they were listed as critically endangered in 2024.

Between about June and November, southern right whales come close to shore along the coast to have their calves.

Khoikhoi and San people lived here for thousands of years before Europeans came. In 1488, the Portuguese sailor Bartolomeu Dias rounded the Cape. In 1652, the Dutch built a supply station so their ships sailing to India and Indonesia could pick up fresh food. It grew into a city.

Later, under the system called [[@apartheid|apartheid]], people were split by skin colour and many families were forced out of their homes. On Robben Island, in the bay, Nelson Mandela spent 18 of his 27 years in prison. Today the island is a museum, and some guides are former prisoners.

sec.h: The city that nearly ran dry
sec.t:
After three very dry years, Cape Town warned in 2018 that its taps might be switched off on "Day Zero". People were limited to 50 litres of water a day each, about what one short shower uses. Families reused bath water to flush toilets. The rains came back, and Day Zero never arrived.

The city also learned some lasting habits. Many homes now collect rainwater in tanks, gardens are planted with plants that need little watering, and hotels ask guests to take two-minute showers. Some families still reuse their bath water. Cape Town is one of several big cities, along with Chennai and São Paulo, that have faced a real risk of their taps running dry in recent years. It showed the world how quickly [[@droughts|droughts]] can threaten even a rich, modern city.
